verses-and-rhymes-by-the-way: The writer known as Norah gathers her poems and rhymes — light verse on travel, nature, and everyday moments noticed along the way. Unpretentious and musical, the collection is the work of a gifted amateur writing for pleasure. Readers who enjoy gentle, old-fashioned poetry will find much to like.
barriers-burned-away: Edward Payson Roe's breakthrough novel unfolds against the Great Chicago Fire of 1871, which literally burns away the barriers between his characters. Through romance tested by disaster, Roe preaches faith, honesty, and the chance to begin again. The book made him famous and remains a vivid picture of nineteenth-century American city life.
wallenstein-s-camp-a-play: Schiller's Wallenstein's Camp — the lively prologue to his great Wallenstein trilogy — shows the imperial general's soldiers carousing, grumbling, and boasting. In one bustling act, the whole Thirty Years War comes alive through its common fighters. A brilliant curtain-raiser to a dramatic masterpiece.
demetrius-a-play: Schiller's unfinished final play dramatizes the mysterious False Dmitri, who claimed the Russian throne in the Time of Troubles. Though death left it incomplete, the surviving scenes show the master's power undimmed. A fascinating fragment from the summit of German drama.
if-i-may: A. A. Milne's If I May gathers his whimsical Punch essays — on holidays, heroes, and the small absurdities of life. His light touch never fails. The perfect bedtime book for grown-ups. Crickets, cousins, and railway carriages all amuse his gentle pen.
toasts-and-forms-of-public-address-for-t: William Pittenger, the Andrews raider turned preacher, offers toasts and forms of public address for all who wish to say the right thing — weddings, banquets, funerals, and public days. Model speeches show the way for nervous orators. A handbook of Victorian eloquence and good manners.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-all-saints-da: A 1913 entry on All Saints' Day — the feast of November first. Francis Mershman traces its history. The Pantheon became Mary's church that day. All heaven is honored at once. The Church's great roll call. Its vigil was once a fast.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ash-wednesday: This 1913 reference article on Ash Wednesday — the opening of the Lenten fast. Herbert Thurston traces its ancient rite. Remember, man, that thou art dust. The ashes mark the brow. The Church's call to penance. Its fast binds the faithful still.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daniel-murray: A 1913 entry on Daniel Murray — the Archbishop of Dublin. Edward D'Alton honors his long primacy. He rebuilt the Irish Church's schools. The emancipation owed him much. The prelate of the Catholic revival. His Dublin pro-cathedral is famed.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-du-coudray: A 1913 entry on Du Coudray — a French officer of note. Thomas Meehan records his American service. The entry preserves his modest fame. His sword served the colonial cause. A soldier of the revolutionary war. His Yorktown service is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edmund-and-jo: A 1913 entry on Edmund and John Hay — the Jesuit brothers. John Hungerford Pollen honors their martyred deaths. They died for the persecuted faith. The entry preserves their blessed memory. The martyrs of the English mission. Their 1579 martyrdom is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-family-of-har: A 1913 entry on the Harlay — the French parlementaires. Georges Goyau notes their famous line. The entry preserves their modest record. Their robes graced the Paris courts. A house of the seventeenth century. Their 1616 presidency is famed.

govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BeckRay_Beck_Ra:
More than three years after the assassination, the FBI's Dallas office still carried an open subject line: Assassination of President John F. Kennedy. This memorandum, dated February 23, 1967, went to SAC Gordon Shanklin, the special agent in charge at Dallas, under file 89-43.

The sender's name is garbled in the scan, a reminder of the condition of much of the released paper. Dallas was where the crime happened, and its office held the local file that every new lead, letter, and claim still entered. The single memo is preserved as a page of that file's long afterlife.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BertrandClayDoc:
Clay Bertrand was the name Jim Garrison's investigation chased through New Orleans: the alleged alias of Clay Shaw, the businessman Garrison put on trial for conspiring to kill President Kennedy. These research notes, dated November 23, 1971, come from a researcher's work on that matter after the trial had ended.

The notes record that Ed Planer confirmed Jesse Core appeared in preserved Johann Rush footage, film connected with Dealey Plaza on the day of the assassination. They also record meetings with Garrison himself. Research notes like these are the workshop floor of assassination scholarship: half-checked leads, names, and film references kept for later use.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MarcusRay_Marcu:
Raymond Marcus published 'Truth vs. Political Truth' as a collection of essays, and this is volume one, dated August 2001. Marcus writes about media elites and how they shape public opinion. His central subject is the assassination of John F. Kennedy and the way it has been covered.

Marcus was a longtime researcher who argued that the press protected the official account. The essays measure news coverage against the evidence as he read it. For readers, the volume offers one researcher's case that political convenience, not proof, settled the story in print. It appeared nearly forty years after Dallas, in a debate that had by then moved from commissions to talk shows and the early internet.
podcast-joerogan-nWY_BXHZNAY:
Author Graham Hancock returns to Joe Rogan for episode 2051 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Hancock is the best known voice for the claim that a high culture fell in the Ice Age. His books and his TV series made the case to a vast crowd.

Hancock gives Rogan his latest form of the case, from new sites to new scans. He argues the proof grows each year while the experts look away. Rogan gives him the long form to lay it all out. Listeners get the claim whole from its top teller. The library keeps the episode as a record of his stated case.
podcast-joerogan-Gm8xFaM-raY:
Sam Harris returns for episode 641 of the Joe Rogan Experience, a middle entry in their long series of talks. Harris, the philosopher and neuroscientist, had by then published widely on religion, ethics, and the mind. His Rogan visits often become the show's most argued-over hours.

The two test their views on free will, moral truth, and how a person should live without faith in old doctrines. Harris keeps his cool, exact manner while Rogan answers from gut and practice. The episode shows their pairing in balance, before later years made Harris a more polarizing figure in Rogan's world.
podcast-joerogan-v2oBLSDCZaY:
Thomas Campbell returns to the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2541, a second long pass at his My Big TOE theory. Campbell, a physicist who worked on missile defense and NASA projects, argues reality is virtual. His model puts consciousness at the center of everything that exists.

Campbell restates the theory in fresh terms and answers the questions his first visit raised. He explains how a computing consciousness could render the world we touch. Rogan probes the testable parts and the spiritual ones. Open-minded listeners get a fuller map of a claim that physics and mysticism rarely share.
nibelungenlied-shumway:
The Nibelungenlied, composed around 1200 by an unknown Austrian poet, is the great heroic epic of the German Middle Ages. Daniel Bussier Shumway's English translation is the text here. It tells of Siegfried the dragon-slayer and the fall of the Burgundian kings.

Siegfried wins the Nibelung treasure and the hand of Kriemhild, then helps King Gunther win the warrior queen Brunhild by stealth. A quarrel of queens ends in Siegfried's murder by the grim Hagen. Kriemhild's revenge, years later at the court of her new husband Etzel, drowns both courts in blood. The poem is Germany's national epic, as stark as any saga.
euripides-alcestis-murray:
Euripides staged Alcestis in Athens in 438 BCE, his earliest surviving play. Gilbert Murray translated the Greek tragedy into English verse. King Admetus may escape death if another person dies in his place.

His wife Alcestis alone accepts the bargain, and the household mourns her deeply. Heracles arrives as a guest, learns the truth, and wrestles Death for her. The play blends grief, gratitude, and an almost comic rescue. It was performed in the slot usually given to a satyr play. Murray's graceful verse keeps its strange, gentle mood intact for English readers.
euripides-electra-murray:
Euripides wrote his Electra around 413 BCE, retelling a story Sophocles also staged. Gilbert Murray translated the tragedy into English verse. Electra lives in exile, married off to a poor farmer, while her mother rules with Aegisthus.

Her brother Orestes returns in secret, and recognition slowly dawns between them. Together they plan the killing of their mother Clytemnestra and her lover. Euripides makes the revenge feel squalid rather than heroic, questioning its justice. Peasant decency contrasts sharply with royal crime throughout. Murray's version brings out the play's bitterness and pity in equal measure.
euripides-hippolytus-bacchae-murray:
Gilbert Murray translated two of Euripides' darkest tragedies in this pairing. Hippolytus dates to 428 BCE, while The Bacchae was produced after the poet's death. Both plays show gods punishing humans who refuse them honor.

Hippolytus spurns Aphrodite, and his stepmother Phaedra's desire destroys them both. In The Bacchae, Dionysus returns to Thebes and drives its women into frenzy. King Pentheus, who denies the god, is torn apart by his own mother. Euripides treats divine power as beautiful and terrifying at once. Murray's verse versions long introduced English readers to these unsettling masterpieces.
euripides-iphigenia-tauris-murray:
Euripides wrote Iphigenia in Tauris around 414 BCE, late in the Trojan War cycle. Gilbert Murray translated the play into English verse. Iphigenia, thought sacrificed by her father, actually serves Artemis in a distant land.

As priestess she must prepare captured strangers for sacrifice on the altar. Two Greeks arrive, and one proves to be her brother Orestes. Brother and sister plot an escape with the goddess's statue in hand. Unlike most tragedies, the play ends in rescue and reunion. Murray renders its suspense and tenderness with unusual charm. Athena herself arrives to bless the escape at the close.
euripides-medea-murray:
Euripides staged Medea in Athens in 431 BCE, at the start of a long war. Gilbert Murray translated the tragedy into English verse. Jason has abandoned Medea, his foreign wife, to marry a Corinthian princess.

Medea pleads, schemes, and finally takes a revenge that still shocks audiences. She kills the princess, the king, and her own two children. Euripides gives her arguments so strong that Jason looks small beside her. The play asks what a wronged outsider owes to law or mercy. Murray's translation carried its power to generations of English readers.
euripides-rhesus-murray:
Rhesus is a short tragedy of a night raid during the Trojan War. Gilbert Murray translated the play, which tradition assigns to Euripides. Modern scholars often doubt that Euripides actually wrote it.

Thracian king Rhesus arrives to aid Troy and camps outside the city walls. Odysseus and Diomedes slip through the dark and kill him in his sleep. A charioteer survives to accuse Hector of betrayal and treachery. The action stays tight, nocturnal, and full of confused alarms. Even as a lesser work, it shows how Greek dramatists mined the Iliad for fresh scenes.
euripides-trojan-women-murray:
Euripides produced The Trojan Women in 415 BCE, while Athens was fighting its own brutal war. Gilbert Murray translated the tragedy into English verse. Troy has fallen, and its royal women wait to be handed to Greek masters.

Hecuba, the widowed queen, watches every remaining hope stripped away. Cassandra is dragged off, Andromache loses her small son to murder, and Helen pleads for her life. Almost nothing happens except suffering, speech by speech. That stillness is the point, and the accusation. Murray's version became famous as an anti-war statement in its own right.
gower-latin-works-macaulay:
George Macaulay's Complete Works of John Gower gathered the poet's writings in four volumes at the turn of the century. Volume Three, from 1902, prints Gower's Latin works with notes. Gower wrote in three tongues, and Latin was his language of public warning.

The chief work here is the Vox Clamantis, the Voice of One Crying, on the Peasants' Revolt of 1381 and the sins of every rank. The Cronica Tripertita treats the fall of Richard II. Shorter Latin poems fill out the volume. Macaulay's editing let English readers meet the stern moralist behind the gentle love poet of the Confessio.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-natal-day: The Church calls a saint's feast his natal day, his birthday into heaven, the day of his death. This entry explains the term, its history, and its liturgical meaning. Dying as a second birth: the martyrs' feasts were the first natal days celebrated.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-new-year-s-da: New Year's Day is the feast of the Circumcision and, since antiquity, of Mary the Mother of God. This entry explains its liturgy, its history, and its customs. The year begins at Mary's side: the octave day of Christmas honors her motherhood.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-norway: Norway was converted by St. Olaf, kept the faith for five centuries, then lost it to the Lutheran Reformation. This entry covers its Catholic history, its shrines, and its modern revival. The land of the midnight sun and the martyr king.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-our-lady-of-a: This entry profiles the shrine of Our Lady of Ambronay, tracing its pilgrims, its miracles, and its place in French devotional life as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact sketch from the encyclopedia's French gallery, preserved among its Marian shrines.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-palm-sunday: Palm Sunday opens Holy Week with Christ's triumphal entry into Jerusalem. This entry explains its liturgy, its procession, and its history. The king acclaimed, the cross ahead: its blessed palms become next year's solemn Lenten ashes quite unfailingly each year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paraguay: Paraguay was the land of the Jesuit reductions, the famous missions among the Guaraní. This entry covers its history, its dioceses, and the reductions' legacy. The faith in the land of the great river: its reductions were a Christian utopia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-passion-sunda: Passion Sunday is the fifth Sunday of Lent, when the crosses are veiled and the Church turns toward Calvary. This entry explains its liturgy, its customs, and its name. The fortnight of the Passion begins: its veils hide the crucifixes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patrick-murra: This biographical entry profiles Patrick Murray, an Irish theologian of the 1800s, tracing his career, his teaching at Maynooth, and his writings as the 1913 editors recorded them. A compact life from the encyclopedia's Irish gallery, preserved among its records of Maynooth's learned professors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-guilla: Frédéric Le Play was the sociologist who studied working-class families across Europe. This entry covers his career, his method, and his Catholic social thought. The father of family sociology: his patient monographs mapped all Europe's working households in loving detail.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reductions-of: The Reductions of Paraguay were the Jesuits' Indian republic. This entry traces their founding, their glory, and their ruin. The utopia of the Guaraní: their ordered villages sang the Catholic faith in Guaraní tongue and song and prayer and work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sainte-anne-d: Sainte Anne d'Auray is the shrine of the Breton pilgrims. This entry covers its basilica, its pardons, and its history. The grandmother's shrine of Brittany: its great pardons draw the Bretons in Morbihan's fields in July's feast of the saint.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sir-john-char: Sir John Charles Day was the judge of the commercial court. This entry notes his bench, his cases, and his fame. The justice of the City merchants: his stern court served the commerce in the 1880s' London in the City.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sunday: Sunday is the Lord's Day of rest. This long entry examines its Sabbath, its Mass, and its law. The first day of the Christian week: its holy rest crowned the faithful in the 300s of the Church in the empire.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thanksgiving-: Thanksgiving Day is the American harvest feast. This entry traces its Pilgrims, its Lincoln, and its history. The holiday of the grateful nation: its laden tables crowned November in the 1863 of the president in the war of the Union.
margret-howth-a-story-of-to-day: A novel by Rebecca Harding Davis, the pioneering American writer of working-class life. Set among ordinary laborers and striving young women, it follows its heroine through hardship, love, and moral choices in an industrializing America. Davis writes with unusual sympathy for the poor, making this an early and earnest voice in the tradition of socially conscious American fiction.
heimskringla-or-the-chronicle-of-the-kin: Written around 1230 by the Icelandic chieftain Snorri Sturluson, this is the great saga-history of Norway's kings. From legendary founders through Olaf the Saint to the Battle of Hastings, Snorri mixes myth, poetry, and hard politics into gripping prose. It is our main source for the Viking Age, and its tales of voyages, feuds, and doomed kings read like the world's first great historical novel.
tono-bungay: H. G. Wells's 1909 novel follows George Ponderevo from a struggling youth to riches built on a worthless patent medicine called Tono-Bungay. Part social satire, part portrait of Edwardian England's money fever, it charts how advertising and ambition hollow out a man's soul. Wells called it his most ambitious novel, and its diagnosis of empty prosperity still bites.
the-round-up-a-romance-of-arizona-noveli: A Western romance novelized from Edmund Day's hit stage melodrama, set on the Arizona range. Cowboy heroics, a plucky heroine, rustlers, and a rousing round-up drive the plot, with all the broad emotion of the theater intact. It is popular entertainment from the heyday of the Western, when the cowboy was America's favorite hero.
sketches-by-boz-illustrative-of-every-da: Dickens's first book, the 1836 sketches that introduced "Boz" to London. Street vendors, cab drivers, cheap theaters, and parish beadles parade through these sharp, funny vignettes of city life. Young, hungry, and brilliantly observant, the twenty-four-year-old Dickens is already unmistakable on every page.
night-and-day: Virginia Woolf's 1919 novel, the most old-style of her books: two young London women weigh love against freedom, home against work. Katherine dreams of the stars while Mary fights for women's rights, and both must pick a path. Calm and finely drawn, it shows Woolf before she broke all the rules.
shelley-an-essay: Francis Thompson's 1908 essay on Shelley, a poet's tribute to a poet. Thompson, himself a visionary Catholic lyricist, finds in Shelley a kindred spirit of beauty and rebellion. Rich, strange, and brilliant, it is criticism as poetry.
ivanoff-a-play: Chekhov's 1887 early play about Ivanov, a landowner sinking into despair and debt. Rawer than his later masterpieces but full of their themes, it shows his genius forming. The young Chekhov finding his voice. Melodramatic in places, but the despair is real and the characters breathe.
the-black-bearded-barbarian-the-life-of-: The life of George Leslie Mackay, the Canadian missionary who brought Christianity and dentistry to Formosa (Taiwan) in the 1870s. His adventures among headhunters, told by Margaret MacGregor, make thrilling reading. A remarkable true story of courage. He faced headhunters and plague with equal courage, and the Formosans loved him for it.
a-wasted-day: A Richard Harding Davis story about a day gone wrong and the lessons it teaches. Light, human, and told with the author's easy charm, it finds meaning in small misadventures. A pleasant minor work. Davis finds the universal in the particular, with a light and practiced hand.
a-millionaire-of-yesterday: An Edward Phillips Oppenheim novel about a self-made millionaire and the dark secrets of his past. Money, mystery, and Edwardian high life unfold in the author's smooth, practiced style. Popular fiction of the first order, with machine-like plotting that never misses a beat.
early-kings-of-norway: Thomas Carlyle's 1875 history of Norway's early kings: Harald Fairhair, Olaf the Saint, and the Viking age. Thunderous and vivid in his prophetic style, it brings the sagas to life. History as epic poetry. Carlyle's Norse heroes stride through these pages like giants.
extracts-from-the-diary-of-william-bray: Extracts from the diary of William Bray, the antiquary who deciphered Pepys's shorthand. Quiet, observant, and full of 18th-century detail, it records a scholar's life. A gentle pleasure for lovers of the period. Bray's quiet industry preserved Pepys for posterity.
how-to-live-on-24-hours-a-day: Arnold Bennett's 1910 self-help classic: how to live fully on twenty-four hours a day. Practical, witty, and wise, it taught clerks to claim their evenings. The most readable time-management book ever written. Bennett's advice is as fresh as when it was written.
man-in-the-iron-mask-an-essay: Dumas's essay on the Man in the Iron Mask: the great historical mystery. Who was the prisoner? His theory, elegantly argued. The classic cold case, dumas ponders history's great mystery, the iron mask, elegantly examined.
the-foundations-an-extravagant-play: Galsworthy cuts loose in this wild play of ideas. Modern England gets a thorough roasting. Satire on a grand, extravagant scale, satire on a grand scale, Galsworthy's wildest, extravagant and sweeping, mocking modern England, Galsworthy's wildest stage work.
the-gilded-age-a-tale-of-today: Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner's 1873 Gilded Age: the novel that named an era. Washington lobbyists and get-rich schemes. The first great American satire.
